catalog_locator: Capell in Coate & Oates 1970:7 (via StressTyp2 passage 1540); Rumsey 1982:9 fn.1, 59
catalog_quote: [StressTyp2 passage 1540, citing Capell 1970:7] Single morpheme words are stressed on the first syllable unless the second has a long vowel. Prefixation does not alter the stress. In four syllable words, an alternative pattern with penultimate stress and initial secondary stress occurs. A suffix does not advance stress in nouns, but in verbs it may. In words consisting of more morphemes the stress is on the root. ... [Rumsey 1982:9 fn.1] For an account of Uŋarinjin stress, see Coate and Oates 1970:7-8. ... [Rumsey 1982:59] A third criterion is that loosely joined elements are stressed independently of the elements to which they are attached, one of the syllables of the postposition always bearing second degree stress (cf. Coate and Oates 1970:78), while tightly joined elements are stressed as part of the word in which they occur, hence often receiving only tertiary stress.
sweep_summary: Ngarinyin (ngar1284, weight-hedged; deciding source Capell 1970:7 known only via StressTyp2 passage 1540). Two title-hits: Capell 1970 'Stress and intonation' (the deciding source) and Coate 1970 'Ngarinjin stress and intonation' tape-transcription booklet. New this sweep: the public archive.org full-text-search API returns scanned highlight fragments from the two access-restricted scans of Coate & Oates 1970, and ~120 chained queries (both scans agree) reconstruct nearly all of pp. 7-8 (saved with raw fragments under. Capell's own words: initial stress in single-morpheme words 'unless there is a long vowel in a subsequent syllable'; long vowels 'tend to attract stress'; length 'not generally phonemic' but 'linked with the stress throughout the language'; prefixation does not alter stress; noun suffixes do not advance stress but verb suffixes may; polymorphemic words stress the root; phrasal verbs stress the auxiliary. This REFINES the catalog: the 'second syllable' window in the StressTyp2 passage is a compiler narrowing (Capell: any subsequent syllable) and the 4-syllable penultimate 'alternative' is StressTyp2's reading of a CvCvCvCv schematic whose marks the scanned lost; the weight-hedged classification stands and is now anchored in the primary text (supersedes the StressTyp2 paraphrase as deciding quote). Coate 1970 booklet: transcript data only (p. 2 facsimile in held Spronck 2015 viewed: interlinear text, no stress marks, no rule), silent, low priority; booklet itself AIATSIS print-only (catalogue Cloudflare-blocked). Rumsey 1982 (held) re-read: defers to Coate & Oates 1970:7-8, confirms. Still unread/paywalled: Jepson & Ennever 2023 (medium), Goedemans 2010 (low). Remaining gap for the page images themselves: the stress diacritics on Capell's CvCvCvCv/CvCvCv displays (medium priority). all lookups were direct fetches.

new_statements.quote: Words consisting of a single morpheme are stressed on the first syllable unless there is a long vowel in a subsequent syllable. While vowel length is not generally phonemic in Ngarinjin, there are certain cases where stress plus length of vowel must be regarded as so [...] In words of this type a syllable containing a long vowel tends to attract stress. Of course, if the first syllable is long stress will fall on it in any case, e.g. 'da:wuru 'beard' or 'e:mundu, 'his mouth'. Prefixation does not alter stress: 'oru, 'his ear', njuno:ru 'her ear'.

In the case of the verb, however, a suffix may advance the stress'). Text obtained as overlapping scanned highlight fragments from the archive.org full-text-search API for both restricted scans (grammarofngarinj0000unse, grammarofngarinj0000coat); page images not opened; the velar nasal is garbled in scanned (njuno:ru = njuŋo:ru).
new_statements.reading: Default initial stress in monomorphemic words, overridden by a long vowel in ANY later syllable (Capell says 'a subsequent syllable', not 'the second'); length is admitted to be only marginally phonemic and 'linked with the stress throughout the language', so the weight condition is real but hedged — exactly the catalog's 'weight-hedged' coding. Polymorphemic words stress the root; noun suffixes never, verb suffixes sometimes, advance stress; prefixes never do. The StressTyp2 clauses 'unless the second has a long vowel' and 'in four syllable words an alternative pattern with penultimate stress and initial secondary stress' are the compilers' verbalisations: the first narrows Capell's window, the second renders his CvCvCvCv/CvCvCv pattern display whose diacritics the scanned did not preserve. Keep catalog_kind weight-hedged; replace the StressTyp2 paraphrase with Capell's wording and widen the weight window from 'second syllable' to 'any non-initial syllable with a long vowel'.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: Rumsey 1982 portions confirmed verbatim in the held lines 915, 3529-3534); the Capell 1970:7 portion exists only as StressTyp2 passage 1540 in, so the deciding text is second-hand and correctly graded carried-quote. Deciding source kind: a 2015 database summary of a 1970 grammar chapter; the 1970 chapter is itself the best description that exists (Rumsey's 1982 reference grammar defers to it; PL C-69 1984, Spronck 2015, and PL 600 2009 -- fetched sources now, silent -- add nothing; no JIPA/instrumental study found), but we do not hold it. Nothing read contradicts the coding ( found the one LHL form a-'ngo:-ni stressed on syllable 2 and HLL 'me:biri on 1, both consistent), and the hedge is honest given root-conditioned placement, the 4-syllable alternative, and Rumsey's argument that vowel length is marginal/non-distinctive. sources.note: Gives no placement rule of its own; defers explicitly to Coate & Oates 1970:7-8 (now read, item 1). Distinguishes primary/secondary/tertiary(=unstressed) stress in the vowel allophony statement, and says a: arises in external sandhi 'only from two stressed vowels' (p.11), consistent with Capell's length-stress linkage. The 'cf. Coate and Oates 1970:78' in the scanned is '7-8'.

sources.quote: No word-stress rule for Ngarinyin. Only an incidental phrase (p.22): mid vowels in Unggumi are rare 'especially within initial stressed syllables such as those shown above' (examples include Ngarinyin degulan, beja, joli), which presupposes initial stress in these words; vowel length status in Proto Worrorran called 'uncertain' (p.25).

The tape and booklet are titled "Ngarinjin - Stress and Intonation"'
sources.note: It is the companion data booklet (interlinear transcription of a 1967 tape) from which Capell drew the passages for his stress-and-intonation section; Coate & Oates 1970 itself says the tape and booklet are available from AIAS. The facsimile of p. 2 that I viewed is plain interlinear text with free translation and no stress or tone marks and no rule prose; Spronck reproduces pp. 2-10 only (about half the booklet). No first-hand stress statement; the remaining ~10 pages are unseen but by description are more transcript.
